text: Across India, millions of older people live on their own at home. When their health starts to slip, the warning signs often appear days before an emergency: fewer steps, poorer sleep, a missed medicine. But no one is watching closely enough to notice.
Aegis Saathi is an early-warning system for seniors living at home. It connects the senior's phone, their care coordinator, and their family, so the right person knows who needs care today.
It starts with a simple phone app for the senior. Big buttons, plain words, and the whole app switches between Hindi and English with one tap.
Each day they tell Saathi how they feel and whether they took their medicine. One tap, and their care manager is told right away.

Saathi also calls them. The check-in call asks about their health, medicine, sleep and appetite, and understands everyday answers. Here, Kamla says she feels dizzy and weak, and slept only four hours.
Now the care coordinator's view. The Today list puts everyone in order of urgency: urgent, needs attention, watch, and stable. Each person comes with the one reason they are on the list.

Open a record, and Saathi explains itself. Sita's steps are eighty-five percent below her own normal, her activity has fallen for five days, and in a call she mentioned pain. Each reason says where it came from.
Readings are compared with each person's own fourteen-day average, not a one-size-fits-all rule, with trends for steps, heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure, sugar, weight and sleep.
Every check-in call lands in the record. The coordinator sees what Saathi heard, the full conversation, and a flag when it thinks they should follow up.
Emergencies come first. When a senior holds the SOS button, the alert reaches the coordinator in seconds, and stays at the top of every page until someone confirms it, or marks it as a false alarm.

The phone can also notice a fall. After a hard impact followed by stillness, it asks the senior if they are okay. If they ask for help, or don't answer within thirty seconds, an emergency alert is raised automatically.
After acting, the coordinator logs a quick follow-up and says whether the alert was useful. Saathi learns from these ratings, so reasons that rarely matter count for less over time.
Operations teams see the whole programme at a glance: people monitored, who needs attention today, open emergencies, response times, and the workload of every coordinator and city.

Accuracy is measured, not claimed. On a simulated validation group, Saathi caught all thirty decline cases, a median of nine days early, with fewer than one false alert per coordinator each week. The limits are listed right on the page.
Families get a calm, simple view, shared only with the senior's consent: how they are today, their steps and medicines this week, and who their care manager is. No scores, and no medical detail.
Aegis Saathi. See who needs care today, before it becomes an emergency.
